C-band 6×6 Dual-Polarised Stacked-Patch Array

S11 / VSWR root-cause analysis with openEMS (FDTD) · project 15_cband-6x6-dualpol-stacked-patch_match-debug · 2026-10-30
Inputs: F_CU.dxf, IN2_CU.dxf, GND.dxf, C_Band_Stackup.pdf · Target band 4–7 GHz

1. Summary

Problem reported: broadside gain is as expected, but the input match is poor; VSWR never gets below 3:1 over 4–7 GHz.
Answer, in short:
  1. The radiating element itself is narrow-band. One element cut out of the board, with its own feed stubs, is matched (VSWR ≤ 3) only from about 5.35 to 6.26 GHz, which is ~16 % bandwidth. The 4–7 GHz target is 54 %. Outside that window most of the power is reflected, so the realised gain drops even though the element still radiates well (its gain referred to accepted power is 8.7–9.8 dBi). That is exactly "gain is OK but VSWR is bad".
  2. The driven patches are edge-fed with no matching. Each feed joins the radiating edge through a 2.48 mm (50 Ω) stub that is only a few mm long. A radiating edge has a resistance of a few hundred ohms. Without the parasitic patch the element is not matched anywhere in 4–7 GHz (worst-case VSWR above 8 everywhere). The parasitic patch is the only reason there is a usable window around 5.8 GHz.
  3. The driven and parasitic resonances merge into one. The parasitics (16.2–17.8 mm) are about the same size as the driven patches (17.07 mm). The simulation shows a single resonance loop, and the matched window simply follows the parasitic size: 16.2 mm gives a window around 5.8 GHz, 18.6 mm moves it down to about 5.0–5.5 GHz, and the window stays narrow in both cases. A broadband stacked patch needs two separate, properly coupled resonances inside the band. This geometry does not have them. Because the parasitics are graded row by row (16.2 to 17.8 mm), each row is matched at a slightly different frequency, so at any one frequency part of the aperture is mismatched.
  4. No feed-network change can fix this on its own. A best-case circuit optimisation on the simulated element impedance (line + transformer + stub) still leaves a worst-case VSWR of about 9 across 4–7 GHz (section 5).
  5. A first redesign iteration did not reach the target yet. An aperture-coupled stacked patch (the usual route to ~50 % bandwidth) was modelled and tuned in 40 full-wave runs (section 7). The best candidate is matched only from about 5.0 to 5.7 GHz, no better than the present element. The study shows why: with air-spaced patches both resonances end up together near 5–5.7 GHz and nothing radiates above ~6 GHz. Section 9 lists what has to change in the next iteration.

ItemValue (from the DXFs)

Array6 × 6, pitch ≈ 44–45 mm (0.59 λ at 4 GHz, 1.03 λ at 7 GHz)

PolarisationDual linear. Port 1 feeds the top/bottom edge of every patch (V-pol); port 2 feeds the left/right edge (H-pol).
Feed networkTwo 36-way corporate networks on In2.Cu. Trace widths: 0.73 mm (≈100 Ω), 1.38 mm (≈70.7 Ω, λ/4 transformers), 2.48 mm (≈50 Ω). Half the patches are fed from the opposite edge, with meander lines for the 180° correction.
PortsOpen ends of the two 2.48 mm launch lines at (−77.6, −2.1) and (−1.5, −2.1) mm. Modelled as 50 Ω coax-like vertical ports.

3. How it was simulated

  • Solver: openEMS v0.37 (FDTD), Gaussian excitation 2.5–8.5 GHz, 8-cell PML on all sides, near-field to far-field box for broadside gain.
  • Geometry read directly from the DXFs (cbgeom.py). Copper is modelled as zero-thickness PEC. RT5880: εr 2.2, tanδ 0.0004. FR4: εr 4.5, tanδ 0.02. The gap is air.
  • Element model (sim_element.py): the row-1/col-1 element is clipped out of In2.Cu with both edge feeds, up to where each becomes a 0.73 mm (100 Ω) branch. Each branch ends in a 100 Ω lumped port. |S11| there is the reflection the element sends into its own branch of the network, and it does not depend on where along the lossless line the cut is made. It sits on a 60 × 60 mm ground with 0.25 mm in-plane cells (2.9 M cells).
  • Full array (sim_array.py): the whole board with both ports, 0.5 mm in-plane cells (12 M cells).
  • Matching study (match_study.py): circuit optimisation on the simulated element impedance.

On the Smith chart the element traces one large, high-Q resonance loop (Fig. 5). It passes through the VSWR 3 circle only between about 5.35 and 6.26 GHz, with a small kink near 5.8 GHz. That kink is the parasitic patch coupling weakly. A well-designed stacked patch shows a tight loop that stays around the centre of the chart across the band. This one does not.

  • B (no parasitic): the bare edge-fed patch is badly mismatched at every frequency. The edge feed was never transformed to the line impedance.
  • C–E (larger parasitic): the matched window moves down in frequency as the parasitic grows, and it gets narrower (16 % at 16.2 mm, 12 % at 18.6 mm, 4 % at 20.3 mm, none at 21.9 mm). Resizing the parasitic tunes where the element works. It does not make it work over 4–7 GHz.

5. Can the feed network alone fix it?

The simulated element impedance was taken from 4 to 7 GHz, and the best possible match was searched for with ideal lossless lines on RT5880 (any impedance 40–150 Ω, any length 0–25 mm):

Matching study on the simulated element (4-7 GHz, 100-ohm branch reference)
A as built                           worst VSWR   28.58   GHz with VSWR<=3: 0.92/3.00   VSWR<=2: 0.37/3.00
B best line + transformer            worst VSWR   13.29   GHz with VSWR<=3: 0.85/3.00   VSWR<=2: 0.55/3.00
C best line + stub + transformer     worst VSWR    9.42   GHz with VSWR<=3: 0.68/3.00   VSWR<=2: 0.00/3.00
B params Z1 150.0 L1 12.28 mm, Z2 103.6 L2 4.64 mm
C params Z1 150.0 L1 7.01, Z2 150.0 L2 20.98, stub Z3 130.4 L3 19.96 mm

No. Even a series line plus a transformer plus a shunt stub leaves a worst-case VSWR of about 9. The element's own reactance swing across 4–7 GHz is too large to compensate with a passive network (Bode–Fano limit). The fix has to be made in the radiator.

6. Full array

Full-array run still in progress. The complete 276.86 mm board (12 M FDTD cells, both 36-way networks, 72 feed points) decays slowly because of the long corporate feed lines: after 10 400 time steps the field energy had only fallen by ~9 dB, so each port needs roughly 35 000–45 000 steps, several hours per port on this PC (16 threads, 7 GB in WSL). Two problems cost the first attempts: the port-2 model put no energy into the board at all, because its port coordinate (x = −1.5081 mm) sat 0.1 µm off the mesh line it should snap to (ports are now rounded to the mesh grid), and the first port-1 run was lost at step 10 400 when three 12 M-cell models shared the memory. S11/S22/S21 will be added in the next revision. The element-level results below already explain the measured behaviour: the array input match cannot be better than the match of the elements it is feeding through a reciprocal, near-lossless corporate network built from 100 Ω branches and 70.7 Ω quarter-wave transformers.

7. Wideband redesign study (first iteration)

Idea. The usual way to reach ~50 % bandwidth with a printed patch is the aperture-coupled stacked patch: the 50 Ω feed line runs under the ground on its own layer and couples to the driven patch through a slot. The slot, the driven patch and the parasitic patch can then each supply a resonance, and the feed layer has room for a matching network. The model (sim_wb_element.py) keeps the present laminates: feed on RT5880 0.8 mm under a slotted ground, air/foam spacer h1, driven patch, air/foam spacer h2, parasitic patch on FR4 0.4 mm. Single polarisation first; the dual-polarised version adds a second, orthogonal slot.

Work done. 40 completed full-wave openEMS runs (0.5 mm cells, 0.8 M cells, 3–12 min each): diagnostics (feed and slot alone, single patch), hand-tuned variants, four generations of a (1+4) evolution strategy over seven dimensions (opt_wb_element.py), a stub-length sweep, and a physics-guided "small driven / large parasitic" round. On top, every candidate was given the best possible feed-layer network (series line + open stub + series line, match_wb.py).

What the study showed

  • The best candidate is no better than the present element yet. It is matched (VSWR ≤ 3) from about 5.0 to 5.7 GHz, a single resonance just like the as-built element.
  • Bare air-spaced patches end up the wrong size. In air a patch for 5–6 GHz must be 20–23 mm. With two patches of nearly the same size the two resonances merge near 5–5.7 GHz, and the upper (anti-phase) mode hardly radiates.
  • Nothing couples above ~6 GHz. For every candidate the input resistance falls to a few ohms between 6 and 7 GHz, whatever the stub length (sweep 4–12 mm). The slot sees no radiating resonator there.
  • Making the driven patch small (to put a resonance near 7 GHz) and the parasitic large (to cover 4.5 GHz) broke the coupling completely with this slot (VSWR > 10 everywhere).
  • A feed-layer network cannot widen a single resonance. For the best candidate the minimax network only spreads the mismatch evenly (worst VSWR 12 → 7) and shrinks the VSWR ≤ 3 window. This is the same Bode–Fano limit as in section 5.
  • The model itself was checked. The feed + slot alone is a nearly lossless load (no radiation, as expected). A single 20 mm patch shows the expected patch resonance near 5.7 GHz. The sharp peaks in the first runs came from the length of line between port and slot, not from a spurious mode.

Conclusion: an aperture-coupled stacked patch is still the right family, but it needs the set-up described in section 9, item 2 (unit cell, dielectric-loaded patches, resonant dog-bone/H slots, a real optimisation budget). The quick air-sheet version tried here does not get there.

8. Root causes, ranked

#CauseEvidenceEffect
1Element bandwidth (~16 %) far below the 54 % targetElement S11, Smith chart, matching studyVSWR > 3 over ~70 % of 4–7 GHz, regardless of the network
2Driven patch edge-fed straight from a 50 Ω stub, with no inset and no transformerVariant B: no match anywhere without the parasiticThe match depends entirely on the parasitic loading
3Driven and parasitic resonances merge (similar sizes, edge feed); the window position is set by the parasitic sizeSingle loop with only a small kink; variants C–E move the window without widening itNo wideband double-tuned response. Rows with different parasitic sizes are matched at different frequencies.
4Element pitch ≈ 44 mm = 1.03 λ at 7 GHzGeometryGrating lobes and gain drop near the top of the band. This affects gain, not S11.

9. What can be done next

In order of priority. Items 1–3 are the work plan for the next iteration; items 4–10 are the design advice from the as-built analysis.

  1. Finish the full-array runs (running now, section 6) and check that the array S11/S22 follow the element curve. That closes the root-cause loop for the existing board.
  2. Second iteration of the wideband element, set up the way published wideband designs are:
    • simulate the element in a unit cell with periodic boundaries at the 44 mm pitch, so the embedded impedance is optimised, not the isolated one;
    • print the patches on thin low-loss carriers (e.g. 0.25–0.5 mm RO4003C/RT5880) over foam instead of bare air sheets. That lowers the patch size and separates the two resonances (lower patch near 6.5–7 GHz, upper patch near 4.3–4.5 GHz);
    • use a near-resonant aperture (dog-bone or H-shaped) that adds a third resonance at the top of the band, and two orthogonal H-slots (or a cross slot with a crossover feed) for dual polarisation;
    • optimise with a proper budget: about 150–250 full-wave evaluations with a surrogate or trust-region optimiser. Each evaluation takes 3–12 min on this PC, so this is one to two days of machine time, or a few hours on a cloud machine.
  3. Keep a more forgiving element type as plan B: an L-probe-fed or four-probe differentially fed patch on ~0.1 λ of foam, or a crossed (bow-tie) dipole over the ground at about λ/4. Dipole-type elements reach 50–60 % bandwidth with high V/H isolation and fit a smaller pitch.
  4. Hold the 4 mm air gap tightly. Check the spacer height on the built board: a 0.3 mm error in a 4 mm gap moves the driven-parasitic coupling noticeably.
  5. Re-tune the element as a true double-resonance stacked patch in a unit-cell (periodic) simulation before touching the network:
    • Separate the two resonances: one near 4.5 GHz and one near 6.5 GHz. That needs the driven patch, the parasitic and the gap (3–6 mm) to be tuned together. Scaling one patch alone only moves a single narrow window (variants C–E).
    • Use the same parasitic size on every row unless a row-by-row taper is deliberately part of the design. The present 16.2–17.8 mm grading detunes the rows from one another.
    • Aim for a tight loop around the chart centre over 4–7 GHz, then use one quarter-wave transformer per element to bring it to 100 Ω.
  6. Change the feed type if 4–7 GHz at VSWR < 2 is required. 54 % bandwidth is very hard for a direct edge-fed stacked patch. Proven routes for this bandwidth are:
    • aperture-coupled stacked patch (H-shaped or cross slots for dual polarisation), with the feed on a separate layer below the ground;
    • L-probe or meandered-probe feed into a thick air/foam patch;
    • a probe-fed stacked patch with capacitive-disc compensation.
    All of these also improve V/H isolation; the edge feeds here couple at only about −7 dB at 7 GHz.
  7. If you keep the edge feed: add an inset or a λ/4 transformer from the edge resistance (100–300 Ω) to 100 Ω on each feed. That centres the existing narrow band on one frequency. It will not widen it to 4–7 GHz.
  8. Reduce the pitch to ≤ 0.7 λ at 7 GHz (≈ 30 mm) if the upper band must be free of grating lobes. This needs the smaller element that a wideband feed allows.
  9. Measurement check: measure S11 of one element on a test coupon and the bare network loaded with 100 Ω resistors. That separates element and network on the bench and confirms this analysis.

10. Limits of this analysis

  • The element was simulated alone on a 60 mm ground. Mutual coupling in the array shifts the embedded impedance a little. The full-array model includes it.
  • The full-array mesh (0.5 mm) snaps the 0.73 mm lines to 0.5 or 1.0 mm, which shifts the network's own resonances by a few percent.
  • Copper thickness, solder mask, connector transitions and the spacers holding the 4 mm gap are not modelled.
  • No measured data was available. The comparison is with the reported symptom (VSWR > 3, gain OK).
